prompt.1: Northern mills are closing, and companies say they cannot get enough wood. How much forest should be cut?
prompt.2: Northern mills are closing, and companies blame a shortage of wood. How should the province decide how much timber is cut?
prompt.3: Northern mills, including Prince George's Northwood pulp mill, are closing, and companies cite fibre supply. How should the harvest be set?
prompt.4: Canfor is closing the Northwood pulp mill, citing pulp losses and fibre supply; the province aims for 45 million cubic metres a year. How should harvest be set?
prompt.5: Canfor will close its Northwood pulp mill (about 300 jobs) in late 2026, citing pulp losses and fibre supply; the Working Forest Landscape Model aims at 45 million cubic metres a year against about 30 million harvested. Which approach?

context.1: Forestry is a main employer in many northern towns. Several mills have closed, and the companies say they cannot get enough wood. The province owns most of the forest and decides how much can be cut. Parties disagree on cutting more, less, or planning differently.
context.2: Canfor announced in July that it will close its Northwood pulp mill in Prince George by the end of 2026, blaming losses and a shortage of wood fibre. The province owns most forest land and sets how much can be cut. The government wants to raise the harvest with a new zoning plan. Parties disagree on how much to cut.
context.3: Canfor announced on July 14, 2026 that its Northwood pulp mill in Prince George will close, citing pulp losses and limited fibre supply. The province's Working Forest plan would split public forest into timber, multiple-use and conservation zones with a goal of 45 million cubic metres a year, up from about 30 million. The Greens reject the plan, CentreBC would write it into law, OneBC would raise the cut, and the Conservatives would set a harvest floor of 45 million.
context.4: Canfor announced on July 14, 2026 the permanent closure of the Northwood pulp mill in Prince George in the fourth quarter, about 300 direct jobs, citing pulp losses and limited BC fibre supply; West Fraser closed its 100 Mile House mill in late 2025. The Council of Forest Industries counts about 15,000 forestry jobs lost since 2022. The government's Working Forest Landscape Model would zone public forest into Working Forest, Multiple Use and Conservation areas with a 'no net loss' rule and a 45 million cubic metre annual harvest objective; the 2025 harvest was about 29 million. The first candidate area, near Campbell River, was announced September 15.
context.5: Canfor announced on July 14, 2026 that the Northwood pulp mill in Prince George will close late this year, affecting about 300 employees, citing pulp losses and limited fibre supply. The Council of Forest Industries counts about 15,000 forestry jobs lost since 2022. The Working Forest Landscape Model would zone public forest into Working Forest, Multiple Use and Conservation areas, with a 'no net loss' provision, 'to stabilize an economic land base that contributes to an annual harvest of 45 million cubic metres'; CentreBC's platform puts the 2025 harvest at 29 million. The first candidate area, near Campbell River, was announced September 15. Party harvest claims (a 'traditional' 60 million; 45 million as a 50% increase) conflict and are not used here.

Its releases do not mention the 45 million figure. No response to Unifor's bridging-to-retirement request.

prompt.1: Gas plants, mines and a power line are planned up north. How should the province decide on them?
prompt.2: Kitimat's gas export plant is doubling, and more plants, mines and a power line are proposed. How should the province handle them?
prompt.3: Kitimat's gas export plant is doubling, and more plants, mines and a power line are proposed. How should the province decide on them?
prompt.4: LNG Canada is doubling; Ksi Lisims LNG is permitted, new mines await permits and the North Coast power line is being built. How should the province handle these projects?
prompt.5: LNG Canada Phase 2 took its final investment decision September 29, 2026, doubling capacity; Ksi Lisims LNG is permitted and heading toward a final investment decision, critical mineral mines await permits, and the North Coast Transmission Line's first phase is under construction. Which approach?

context.1: The north has big projects waiting: gas export plants, new mines, and a long power line to run them. The province decides whether and how fast to approve them, and what pollution and First Nations rules apply. Parties disagree on speed and conditions.
context.2: In September the companies behind the Kitimat gas export plant agreed to build a second phase. Another gas plant near Prince Rupert has its permits but no final go-ahead, new mines are waiting on permits, and construction has started on a north coast power line. The province sets approval timelines, pollution rules, the carbon price for industry, and First Nations partnership rules. Parties disagree on speed and conditions.
context.3: The Kitimat gas export plant's owners are doubling it after a September decision. The Ksi Lisims plant near Prince Rupert is permitted but awaits its investment decision, mine proposals are in the permit queue, and the first phase of the North Coast power line is under construction. The NDP requires new plants to be net-zero ready by 2030. The Conservatives would legislate 120-day approvals and drop emissions limits. CentreBC would set a one-year legal deadline. The Greens would approve no new gas plants.
context.4: LNG Canada announced its Phase 2 final investment decision on September 29, doubling Kitimat capacity to 28 million tonnes. The NDP requires new projects to be net-zero ready by 2030, would run assessments and permits at the same time, double mineral exports and fast-track the North Coast line with Canadian steel. The Conservatives' plan doubles gas production by 2032, ends emissions limits, legislates 120-day permits and sets a fixed deadline for the line. CentreBC backs LNG with First Nations partners and net-zero plans, a 12-month decision deadline and ten mine decisions by 2030. The Greens would end approvals for new LNG and pipelines.
context.5: LNG Canada's Phase 2 final investment decision (September 29, 2026) doubles Kitimat capacity to 28 million tonnes. On the NDP's own numbers, capacity reaches nearly 48 million tonnes by 2035, above the Conservatives' 'triple by 2035' target, so the NDP and the Conservatives differ mainly on conditions and process. The NDP pledges to double critical mineral exports in five years, run permits concurrently, build the North Coast Transmission Line with Canadian steel, and keep the net-zero-ready requirement. The Conservatives would double gas by 2032 and triple by 2035, end emissions limits, pass a 120 Day Permitting Act and fix a line deadline. CentreBC requires First Nations partners and credible net-zero plans, keeps industrial carbon pricing, sets a 12-month provincial deadline and promises decisions on 10 mines by 2030. The Greens would approve no new LNG or pipelines.

context.1: In many northern towns the hospital emergency room shuts for hours or days because no doctor or nurse can staff it. People drive long distances for help. The province pays for hospitals and decides how to attract staff. Parties disagree on what would work fastest.
context.2: Small northern hospitals closed their emergency rooms repeatedly in 2026 because of staff shortages, including Fort St. James, Hudson's Hope, Chetwynd and 100 Mile House. In March the northeast lost 115 hours of emergency and maternity care. The province has opened hospitals in Terrace and Fort St. James, but staffing them is the problem. Parties disagree on the fix.
context.3: Northern Health reported 115 hours of emergency or maternity closures in northeast BC in March 2026, including 60 hours at Hudson's Hope, citing staffing. Fort St. James closed again on May 26, and 100 Mile House, in Interior Health, had closed 38 times by late August. The Conservatives launched a $50 million rural fund in 100 Mile House on October 5. CentreBC promises a closure-reporting law and a yearly fund. The NDP offers tuition and moving help for rural work and would phase out private agency nurses.
context.4: Northern Health logged 115 hours of emergency or related closures in northeast BC in March 2026 (Hudson's Hope 60), citing staffing. Fort St. James closed again on May 26; Interior Health's 100 Mile House emergency room had closed 38 times by August 24. New hospitals opened in Terrace (2024), Fort St. James (2025) and Prince Rupert (2025), but staffing drives the closures. The Conservatives launched a $50 million rural practice fund with flexible staffing in 100 Mile House on October 5. CentreBC promises an accountability law and a $25 million a year fund. The NDP offers rural tuition, loan forgiveness and moving support, and would phase out private agency nurses (October 12). context.5: Northern Health reported 115 hours of emergency or related closures in northeast BC in March 2026, including 60 at Hudson's Hope, with staffing the stated cause. Fort St. James closed again on May 26, and Interior Health's 100 Mile House emergency room had closed 38 times by August 24. The Conservatives pledge a $50 million rural practice fund, flexible staffing, automatic credential recognition and an expert commission (October 5, 100 Mile House); CentreBC an Emergency Room Accountability Act, halved unplanned closure hours by 2029/30, a $25 million a year fund and a permanent retention bonus; the NDP rural tuition discounts, loan forgiveness, moving costs and 1,000 nursing and care training seats (October 9) and a three-year phase-out of private agency nurses with savings to rural travel nurses (October 12); the Greens a community health centre per riding and a review toward a single authority; OneBC private care alongside public.
